slides.title: Origins
slides.sub: Three stories that explain why Bitcoin looks the way it does
slides.notes: Three stories explain why Bitcoin looks the way it does: a newspaper headline carved into the first block, the first purchase made with bitcoin, and forty years of failed attempts at digital money. Each story is dated and sourced on its own slide.

slides.title: A newspaper headline carved into block zero
slides.sub: Recorded: 3 January 2009

items.cap: Recorded: block 0's real 285 bytes, fetched from the live chain for this deck; its hash re-verified in the build

items.headline: Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks

items: The orange bytes ARE the headline

items.linkText: Genesis block coinbase, with the headline (tx)

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 3 January 2009. The first Bitcoin block ever mined carries a piece of that morning's newspaper: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'. It proves the block could not have been made earlier than that headline, and at the same time records why the system was built - in the middle of a banking crisis, by someone who wanted money that needs no bailout and no bank. The source is Bitcoin genesis block coinbase text, block 0, 2009-01-03; The Times front page of 3 January 2009; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin (genesis block).
slides.take: History is written into the chain itself

slides.title: The first person ever paid in bitcoin
slides.sub: Satoshi Nakamoto, and the cryptographer who ran the code

items.cap: anonymity, from the owner's 2025 deck

items: Satoshi Nakamoto: still unidentified, by design
Hal Finney answered the whitepaper - and 'Running bitcoin'
Block 170, January 2009: Satoshi pays Finney 10 BTC

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated January 2009. Nine days after the genesis block, Satoshi Nakamoto sent 10 bitcoin to Hal Finney, a veteran cryptographer who had answered the whitepaper with curiosity instead of dismissal and famously tweeted 'Running bitcoin'. Finney had worked on PGP and had built the first reusable proof-of-work system years before Bitcoin existed - the first payment went to someone who had spent a career preparing for it. The source is Bitcoin block 170, 2009-01-12, the first bitcoin transaction (Satoshi Nakamoto to Hal Finney, 10 BTC); Hal Finney, 'Running bitcoin', twitter.com/halfin, 2009-01-10.
slides.take: Peer to peer meant person to person from day one

slides.title: Forty years of failed digital money
slides.sub: Every part existed before Bitcoin combined them

items: DigiCash went bankrupt; b-money and bit gold were never built - agreement without a leader was missing

items.who: Chaum, Back, Dai, Szabo - then Nakamoto

slides.notes: Bitcoin was not the first attempt at digital money. David Chaum's blind-signature ecash of the 1980s ended with the bankruptcy of his company DigiCash, and Adam Back's Hashcash of 1997 priced email spam with proof of work. Wei Dai's b-money and Nick Szabo's bit gold, both of 1998, were never built because neither could agree on a history without a leader. The sources are Nakamoto's 2008 paper and the original text of each author.
slides.take: The pieces were old; the combination was new

slides.title: Money
slides.sub: What the currency is, who issues it, and on what schedule

items.cap: Lydian electrum, the first coins - photo: brewbooks, CC BY-SA 2.0

slides.notes: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Money.

slides.title: The island where money never moved
slides.sub: Yap, documented 1903

items.cap: a rai stone on Yap - photo: Eric Guinther, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: Rai stones were money too heavy to move, so they never moved
A payment was the village agreeing the owner had changed
One stone sank at sea - and kept changing owners anyway

items.cap: the stone stays; only the shared record moves

items.who: the Yapese; documented by anthropologist W. H. Furness III
items.linkText: Furness: The Island of Stone Money (book)

slides.notes: On the island of Yap, wealth was held in rai, limestone discs up to four metres wide and far too heavy to move. When a stone changed owners it stayed where it lay, and only the community's shared memory of who owned it changed. That is a ledger without a bank, the idea Bitcoin rebuilds. The sources are Furness, The Island of Stone Money (1910), and Milton Friedman's Hoover working paper of 1991 with the same title.
slides.take: Money is a ledger; Bitcoin makes it digital

slides.title: Five thousand years to digital cash

items.cap: a barley account, Sumer - Met, CC0
electrum stater, 600-550 BCE - CMA, CC0

items.body: The oldest money we can hold is already a ledger entry (left) and a standard token (right).

items.who: ledger-keepers, from temple scribes to central banks

slides.notes: Money has changed form many times: grain-ledger entries in Mesopotamia, the first struck coins in Lydia around 600 BCE, paper notes in Song-dynasty China, and goldsmiths' receipts that became bank money. In 1971 the dollar's last tie to gold was cut, leaving pure fiat money. Bitcoin is the next step in that sequence, money that exists only as digital records. The sources are standard monetary histories and chapter 1 of Mastering Bitcoin, third edition.
slides.lede: Those Lydian coins were money once; so is your app balance - the difference is always the ledger.
slides.take: Each era changed the ledger-keeper; Bitcoin removed the position

Peer to peer, in about an hour

slides.notes: The table compares traditional cash, digital money held at banks and cryptocurrency on who issues it, where it exists and who keeps the ledger. The remaining rows ask what sets the supply and how a payment settles. Read down a column to see one kind of money, and across a row to see which property changes. The difference in who keeps the ledger is the subject of this course.
slides.take: Same uses, different ledgers - and that difference is this course

slides.title: Physical cash: superb in person, stuck there
slides.sub: Why the oldest form still works - and where it stops

left.head: What cash does well
rows: Settles hand to hand, instantly and finally
Needs no account, bank, identity, or permission
Cannot be frozen or censored remotely

right.head: Where it fails
rows: Cannot travel a wire - no remote commerce
Theft and loss are final; carrying value is risky

slides.notes: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: which of these failures did cards fix? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Money.
slides.lede: Before praising Bitcoin, be fair to cash: it settles instantly, anonymously, with no middleman - but it cannot reach the internet.
slides.take: Cash is a bearer instrument: perfect in person, useless on a network

slides.title: The internet got payments - and new gatekeepers
slides.sub: The dot-com boom digitised paying, not cash

items.label: Beenz and Flooz die with the crash

items: What survived was account money on one company's ledger - convenient, reversible, and censorable

items.who: Max Levchin and Peter Thiel (Confinity), Elon Musk (X.com)
items.where: Palo Alto, in the dot-com boom

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 1998 - 2002. The web could sell before it could pay: cards were unsafe to type and banks had no internet rails. Confinity, founded 1998 by Max Levchin and Peter Thiel, and X.com, founded 1999 by Elon Musk, raced to fix it, merged in 2000, and became PayPal - sold to eBay for 1.5 billion dollars in 2002. The source is en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PayPal (Confinity 1998, X.com 1999, merger 2000, eBay acquisition 2002); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flooz.com and /wiki/Beenz.com (both closed 2001 in the dot-com crash).
slides.lede: Before asking why Bitcoin exists, remember the dot-com race: the web needed money, companies built it as accounts - and the failures took their users' balances down with them.
slides.take: Payments went online in 1998-2002; cash never did

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.sub: Five documented cases, five links - no hypotheticals

items.text: No banks for most adults - M-Pesa made phones the payment rail
Banks shut for days; a levy took part of deposits overnight
Capital controls: ATM withdrawals capped at 60 euros a day
Hyperinflation beyond 1,000,000% - wages melted in hours
Under invasion, the state itself raised ~$35M in crypto in a week

items.body: photos via Wikimedia Commons: Fiona Graham/WorldRemit CC BY-SA 2.0 · Martin Addison CC BY-SA 2.0 · Norbert Nagel CC BY-SA 3.0 · Rjcastillo CC BY-SA 4.0 · U.S. Embassy Kyiv (PD)

items.who: savers, the unbanked, and one government under invasion

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2007 - 2022. Money fails people in documented ways. Kenya, 2007: most adults had no bank, so Safaricom's M-Pesa turned phone credit into the country's money rail. The source is en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Pesa (Safaricom, 2007); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012-2013_Cypriot_financial_crisis (deposit levy, March 2013); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_government-debt_crisis (2015 capital controls, 60-euro limit); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Venezuela (over 1,000,000% in 2018); CNBC 2022-03-02 and Fortune 2022-03-26 on Ukraine's official crypto donations (Alex Bornyakov, 35 million dollars within the first week).
slides.lede: E-commerce without cards, aid without banks, savings under levies, wages under hyperinflation, a state under invasion: each card below is a real, dated case with its source.
slides.take: Crisis or war, banked or not - the need is documented, not theoretical

slides.title: Why digital money had to wait
slides.sub: The copy problem: a digital coin is a file

items: Make money digital and it becomes a file
Files copy perfectly - so coins would too
Both copies get spent: the double-spend
For decades only a trusted central ledger could stop it - so digital money meant bank money

slides.notes: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why does the same problem not exist for paper cash? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Double spend.
slides.lede: Digital money is older than you think - what was missing for forty years was a way to stop one coin being spent twice without a bank in the middle.
slides.take: Perfect copies made digital cash impossible without a referee

slides.title: The double-spend, solved in public
slides.sub: One shared ledger, one agreed order - no referee needed

items: Every payment is broadcast to every node
Nodes agree on one order for all payments
The first spend of a coin enters the block
The second is refused by every node, everywhere

slides.notes: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: what stops the network agreeing on the WRONG order? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Double spend and Consensus.
slides.lede: Satoshi's whitepaper names the problem in its second sentence; the answer is not better files but a public ledger every node keeps and orders together.
slides.take: The referee is everyone, and the whistle is arithmetic

slides.notes: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). slides.title: Two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoin

items.label: offered on the bitcointalk forum by Laszlo Hanyecz

items.cap: photo: Valerio Capello, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: For 18 months bitcoin ran with no known price at all
Someone took the offer and ordered him two pizzas
The first commercial purchase gave bitcoin its first real price
22 May is still celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 22 May 2010. For Bitcoin's first year and a half, nobody knew what a bitcoin was worth, because nobody had ever bought anything with one. Then Laszlo Hanyecz, a Florida programmer, offered 10,000 BTC on a forum to anyone who would bring him two pizzas - and someone did. The source is Guinness World Records, 'First commercial Bitcoin transaction' (Laszlo Hanyecz, 2010-05-22, 10,000 BTC for two pizzas); bitcointalk.org thread 'Pizza for bitcoins?', May 2010.
slides.take: Price is discovered the first time someone pays

slides.title: Peers find each other without a directory
slides.sub: The chapter's own protocol sketch - run, not quoted

items: One peer starts, knowing two neighbours
Each round it asks the peers just found for THEIR neighbours
Rounds are counted until all seven peers are known: 4

items.cap: what it builds: a flat mesh

items.label: rounds of gossip until every peer is known - no server, no registry

lines: frontier = {n for f in frontier for n in links[f]} - seen
items.cap: program PeerToPeerProtocol, lines 1 to 6 of 6, run under Python 3.14.6
items.label: the exact program - run it at home

slides.notes: One peer starts out knowing two neighbours, and in each round it asks the peers it has just found for their neighbours. The program counts the rounds of gossip until all seven peers are known, and it reports four. No server or registry is involved, which is why the network needs no directory.
slides.take: The network is just nodes agreeing to speak alike

slides.title: Your key is your deed - and you may never show it
slides.sub: The house-key analogy, and where it breaks

items: Bitcoin's trick (ch. 4 and 8): a signature proves you hold the key while the key itself stays secret

slides.notes: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs. Think about this case: your house has a registry if the key is lost. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Key control.
slides.lede: With a car or a house, the key grants access but a registry proves ownership; in Bitcoin the key is both - so it must prove without being shown.
slides.take: Prove you hold the key; never reveal it

slides.title: Mt. Gox: the exchange that lost everyone's coins
slides.sub: NOT EXECUTED: Tokyo, February 2014 - figures from the court filing, not recomputed

items.label: bitcoins missing per the Tokyo court filing, Feb 2014
Mt. Gox had been the largest bitcoin exchange in the world
creditors still being repaid a decade later

items: Customers saw balances on a website; the keys - so the coins - sat in one company's safe
When the keys vanished, every balance on the screen meant nothing

items.who: Mt. Gox, led by CEO Mark Karpeles
items.where: Tokyo; bankruptcy filed at the Tokyo District Court

slides.notes: The exchange Mt Gox of Tokyo, led by Mark Karpeles, was once the largest bitcoin exchange in the world. In February 2014 it halted withdrawals, filed for bankruptcy and admitted that about 850,000 bitcoins were gone. Customers had balances on a website, but the keys, and therefore the coins, had been in someone else's hands all along. The figure comes from the Tokyo District Court filing of 28 February 2014 and is reported here, not recomputed.
slides.lede: Not a parable: a named company, a named CEO, a dated court filing - and the course's first security lesson.
slides.take: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins - exchanges included

slides.title: From a phrase to a key, slowly on purpose
slides.sub: Key stretching makes guessing expensive

items: Start from a human backup phrase and a salt
Hash them with HMAC-SHA512 - that is one round
Feed each round into the next, 2,048 times
Result: a 64-byte seed; a guesser pays the 2,048 rounds for every guess

items.cap: result: a 64-byte seed, digest d96147bf

lines: seed = bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(seed, u))

slides.title: Two solved problems, one new system
slides.sub: 1997 and 1982 meet in 2008

items.head: Hashcash (1997)
items.body: Proof-of-work: make sending cost a computation, so flooding costs real resources. Bitcoin turns the same cost into the price of writing history.

items.head: Byzantine Generals (1982)
items.body: How do parties that cannot trust each other agree on one message? Proof-of-work plus the longest valid chain is Bitcoin's practical answer.

slides.notes: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it. The block is a group of transactions that the network accepts together, the blockchain is the list of blocks linked one to the next, the timestamp is the mark of time that orders them, and the node is a computer that takes part in the network. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Chain and Cryptography.

slides.notes: The Transfer section explains what happens when Joe sends bitcoin to Alice. It follows the payment from the moment he presses Send to the moment it is confirmed in a block, and it introduces the objects and ideas involved: the transaction, its inputs and outputs, the fee, the confirmation, the irreversibility, and the newer payments that never reach the public chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Transfer and Semantic bridge.
slides.take: The chain settles; the edges scale

slides.title: The chapter in six lines
slides.sub: One line per part - each one provable from its slides

items: Origins: a dated newspaper headline sits in block 0, and the first payment went person to person
Money is a ledger: five thousand years of forms, three kinds today - what differs is who keeps it
Supply: 21 million by arithmetic - halvings on real, chain-stamped dates; a sum anyone can re-run
Price: discovered by trades, never declared - from two pizzas to $854M on one log chart
Network: no bank in the middle - every node checks every rule, and mining pays for honesty
Wallets: whoever holds the keys holds the coins - Mt. Gox is the named, dated proof

slides.notes: Six lines, one per part. If any of them still feels like a claim rather than a fact, the agenda slide names the slides that prove it - and the course page carries the full text. A question to think about is this: which line would you defend to a sceptic first, and with which slide? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in every section.
